content: The pinworm, scientifically classified under the genus Enterobius, is a parasitic nematode (roundworm) that commonly infects the human gastrointestinal tract. In the United Kingdom and Australia, it is also referred to as the threadworm, while in some contexts, it is called the seatworm. The medical condition caused by pinworm infestation is termed enterobiasis, a type of helminthiasis. Less precisely, it is sometimes referred to as oxyuriasis, in reference to the family Oxyuridae. For the purposes of this discussion, the term pinworm will specifically denote Enterobius species. However, in British usage, pinworm refers to Strongyloides, while Enterobius is called threadworm. The pinworm is a type of roundworm, and three species within the genus Enterobius have been definitively identified. Humans are exclusively hosts to Enterobius vermicularis (formerly known as Oxyurias vermicularis). Chimpanzees, on the other hand, are hosts to Enterobius anthropopitheci, which is morphologically distinct from the human pinworm. There is some debate regarding the existence of another species, Enterobius gregorii, which has been proposed as a sister species to E. vermicularis. However, its status as a separate species remains controversial. Some researchers argue that E. gregorii represents a younger developmental stage of E. vermicularis. Clinically, E. gregorii is considered identical to E. vermicularis. Adult female pinworms measure approximately 8–13 mm in length and 0.5 mm in thickness, while males are smaller, measuring 2–5 mm in length and 0.2 mm in thickness, with a curved posterior end. Pinworm eggs are translucent, adhesive, and measure 50–60 μm by 20–30 μm. They have a thick shell flattened on one side. Due to their small size and colorless nature, the eggs are invisible to the naked eye unless present in large clumps. Eggs may contain either a developing embryo or a fully developed pinworm larva, which grows to a length of 140–150 μm. Pinworm infection is the most common helminthic (parasitic worm) infection in the United States, Western Europe, and Oceania. Prevalence rates vary, with estimates of 4% among people of all ages. Children are particularly susceptible, with reported prevalence rates as high as 61% in India, 50% in England, 39% in Thailand, 37% in Sweden, and 29% in Denmark. Behaviors such as finger-sucking and nail-biting are associated with increased incidence and relapse rates. Pinworms are easily transmitted among individuals living in close contact, such as within households, and tend to infect all members of a household. The prevalence of pinworms is not associated with gender, social class, race, or culture, making them an exception to the general rule that intestinal parasites are less common in affluent communities. The earliest known evidence of pinworm infection in humans dates back to 7837 BC, as evidenced by pinworm eggs found in coprolite (fossilized feces) in western Utah. However, parasitic pinworm nematodes were already present 240 million years ago, as indicated by a fossilized egg found in the dung of pre-mammalian cynodonts. The pinworm's entire life cycle occurs within the gastrointestinal tract of a single human host and spans approximately 2–4 weeks or 4–8 weeks. The cycle begins when eggs are ingested. Once in the duodenum (the first part of the small intestine), the eggs hatch, and the emerging larvae grow rapidly to a size of 140–150 μm. The larvae then migrate through the small intestine toward the colon, undergoing two molts to become adults. Female pinworms live for 5–13 weeks, while males survive for about 7 weeks. Mating occurs in the ileum (the last part of the small intestine), after which male pinworms die and are excreted in the stool. Gravid (egg-carrying) females migrate to the cecum (the beginning of the large intestine), appendix, and ascending colon, where they attach to the mucosa and feed on colonic contents. A gravid female's body becomes almost entirely filled with eggs, with estimates ranging from 11,000 to 16,000 eggs per female. Approximately five weeks after the initial ingestion of eggs, gravid females migrate through the colon toward the rectum at a rate of 12–14 cm per hour. They emerge from the anus and deposit eggs on the perianal skin. This process may occur through contraction and expulsion of eggs, disintegration of the female worm, or bodily rupture caused by the host scratching the worm. After depositing eggs, the female becomes opaque and dies. The emergence of the female from the anus is thought to provide the oxygen necessary for egg maturation. The primary symptom of pinworm infection (Enterobius vermicularis) is anal itching. First-line treatment includes albendazole or mebendazole, with pyrantel pamoate as an alternative. Pinworm eggs are highly infectious and can survive in a moist environment for up to three weeks. They are sensitive to heat but can withstand low temperatures, with two-thirds of eggs remaining viable after 18 hours at −8°C (18°F). Eggs are readily transmitted to other surfaces through contamination. Their sticky surface allows them to adhere to fingernails, hands, nightclothing, and bed linen. From these surfaces, eggs can be further transmitted to food, water, furniture, toys, bathroom fixtures, and other objects. Household pets may carry eggs in their fur without being infected. Dust containing eggs can become airborne and widely dispersed, for example, when bedclothes and linen are shaken. Consequently, eggs can enter the mouth and nose through inhalation and be swallowed. Although pinworms do not multiply within the human host, some larvae may hatch on the anal mucosa and migrate back into the gastrointestinal tract in a process called retroinfection. Retroinfection can lead to a heavy parasitic load and perpetuate the infestation. To completely eradicate the infection, repeated treatment at two-week intervals is often necessary. Pinworms are sometimes diagnosed incidentally during pathological examinations. Microscopic analysis can reveal pinworms in the appendix or their eggs under a light microscope. High-magnification micrographs may show the cephalic alae (head structures) of Enterobius vermicularis or the ultrastructural details of their eggs.
